

**Technical mentor allocation: the gated claim model**

**RECOMMENDATION**

Adopt a gated claim model. Teams self-select their technical mentor, and the first claim locks an exclusive three-session pairing. Self-selection governs entry and choice; assignment-grade continuity follows automatically. There is no matching engine and no administrative queue — only a gate, a claim, a cap and a counter.

The constraint is real: **120 technical mentors against a nominal 2,500 teams is 1 mentor to 21 teams**, where cohort mentoring works at 1:5 to 1:8. No allocation rule closes that gap. What the design can do is spend capacity only on teams that have proved they exist, preserve continuity where nearly all the value of three short sessions lies, and recover capacity that popularity effects and defensive claiming would waste.

![][image1]

**HOW IT WORKS**

| Gate | Technical mentor access unlocks when a team submits a proposal against a confirmed brief. Not on request, not at team formation. |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Browse** | Filtered by build capability — retrieval/RAG, computer vision, speech and ASR, tabular ML, agents, fine-tuning, mobile and edge, data engineering — not by sector. Standardised profiles; no employer logos, seniority ranking or ratings. |
| **Claim** | First team to claim locks the mentor for all three sessions; the team books individual slots in that mentor’s calendar. Proposal auto-attached at claim, and each booking requires one line: the specific question the team wants answered. |
| **Caps** | Maximum three live claims per mentor regardless of declared capacity. Slots reopen as pairings complete. Pool released in waves. |
| **Expiry** | Session one must be scheduled within 14 days of claim, or the claim lapses and the mentor returns to the pool. The team may re-claim, behind fresh teams. Stated at claim time. |
| **Exit** | One no-fault team-initiated swap after session one; mentor-initiated release; automatic release after 10 days of mentor non-response. |
| **Stipend** | Paid per session delivered, not per team completed. $2.67/session is budget-neutral against $8/team; the mentor line appears sized for c.250 mentors, so there is headroom to go to $4–5 and use it in the Wave 3 pitch. |

![][image2]

**WHY NOT THE TWO OPTIONS ORIGINALLY CONSIDERED**

**Ask and auto-assign.** “Do you need a mentor?” is free to answer yes to, so it collects a signal with no information in it — expect 70–90% yes. Assignment is not engagement: auto-matched pairs in volunteer programmes routinely see 40–60% never holding session one, and a completion-tied stipend makes the mentor bear that cost.

**Unstructured Open per-session booking.** Three different mentors destroys continuity — sessions two and three are spent re-establishing context. Teams choose on legible proxies such as job title and employer brand, so recognisable names are swamped while equally capable mentors sit idle, and the teams needing help most book least. It also carries a hidden queue of cancellations, reschedules and no-show adjudication that nobody owns.

**THE EARLY-ASSIGNMENT CONCERN**

**On the mentor side this is a real risk and correctly identified.** Wave 3 recruitment lands August–September; first proposals arrive months later. A dormant window between onboarding a volunteer and giving them anything to do is the likeliest route to arriving at the build phase with 80 effective mentors rather than 120\.

**On the team side it is not.** Pre-proposal teams are not unsupported — the problem owner is running the walkthrough, which is the right help at that stage. Early assignment cannot fix engagement for teams that have not yet formed or chosen a brief; it simply allocates scarce capacity to teams that may never submit.

**The fix is not an earlier assignment but earlier activity.** Give mentors work during the gap: capability clinics, guest slots in the Thursday AI School sessions, capability channels on Discord, and proposal review. Mentors stay warm, teams get earlier technical exposure, and the hours count toward the mentorship indicator. Early assignment burns capacity; early activity builds it.

**COVERAGE, STATED HONESTLY**

The model produces roughly 600 dedicated pairings against a nominal 2,500 teams. That is acceptable: 2,500 is a registration-derived denominator, and the indicator matrix puts MVP submission at 500–1,000. The gate rations capacity against the population that actually reaches the proposal. Below the 1:1 tier, mentorship is tiered rather than binary.

| Dedicated mentor | 1 : 1 | Teams that reach the proposal stage and claim. Three sessions, same mentor, exclusive. |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Capability clinics** | **c. 1 : 12** | All teams. Mentor-led drop-in sessions grouped by build capability. |
| **Async channels** | **many : many** | All teams. Capability channels on Discord, monitored by mentors on rota. |
